catalog_quote: Regardless of word class, the stress on the word root is regularly on the penultimate syllable. ... (97) /bakala/ [ba.ˈka.la] ‘wide canoe paddle’ ... (99) /maɲahaɣei/ [ma.ɲa.ˈha.ɣei] ‘want, desire’ ... An expectation of total uniformity regarding the underlying penultimate stress rule on word roots is incorrect. During a period of almost three decades of listening to conversations, I have noted that occasional words deviate from the stress rule and have acquired their own stress patterns, and there is no apparent reason for the variation ... The inventory of words which show this variation is low ... 2.9.2 Stress in morphologically complex words Within derived words, the word root maintains penultimate syllable stress, but any additional suffixes or clitics also bear final stress. ... (106) /ma.ɲa.ˈha.ɣei.ˈni/ magnahagei=ni ‘want/desire=3SG.OBJ’ (107) /ma.ɲa.ˈha.ɣei.ni.ˈhi/magnahagei=ni…

audit.reasoning: The classification (root-penultimate stress, weight-blind, with additional stress on the word-final enclitic/suffix, causative fa- and reduplication not shifting root stress, a small listed set of lexical exceptions) rests on the dedicated stress section (2.9, pp. 35-37) of the only reference grammar of the language, Boswell 2018 (LOT 518, open access), which we hold; every quoted fragment was re-located verbatim in the held text at the cited sections/pages, and the p. 12 and p. 55 summaries match. Glottolog's descriptive bibliography has nothing better (2 refs: this grammar and a syntax article), web search turned up no phonology monograph or instrumental study, and the one other substantial description (White et al. 1988 PL C-97, fetched sources now and is silent on stress. The description is impressionistic rather than acoustic
